item.title: The “just kidding” heard around the world
item.dc:creator: Whizy Kim
item.description: Jensen Huang is Nvidia’s CEO again, less than a week after the company’s board swore he wouldn’t return.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: The “Days Since Jensen Was CEO” counter has officially reset to zero. Less than a week after Nvidia said it was never, ever getting back together with Jensen Huang, the board has unanimously voted to give him a second shot at the CEO job, effective immediately (here’s what members had to say). The encore follows a big push from the US president—and a bruising tech stock sell-off last week.

What happened: This reversal comes just 11 days after Huang resigned following his admission of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy named Alice Huang (reminder: no relation). This makes his timeout one of the shortest CEO exits on record, right up there with Sam Altman’s five days of unemployment in 2023.

Despite allegations of multiple extramarital affairs (including at least two with Nvidia employees) and reports that the board was disturbed by Huang’s “lying” and “lack of candor,” the on-and-off CEO had his fair share of defenders. Most prominent among them: President Donald Trump, who told CNBC he spoke to the board himself and “made the deal” to bring Huang back.

More Stories

Tech Business

Who’s going to steer the chips?

AI

Apple finally RSVPs to the AI agent party

Consumer Electronics

Turning the page on my old Kindle

Nvidia’s board put it more vaguely, saying its decision came after “input from senior levels of the United States government” and that it’s “confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” The board clearly had its reasons for bringing Huang back, and last week’s tech sell-off may have played a part. Either way, investors approved, and Nvidia’s stock jumped more than 30% when the news broke.

Meanwhile, in Washington: Huang may be back as CEO, but the investigations surrounding him are still underway (including the Nvidia board’s own independent probe, which it reiterated will continue). The Justice and Commerce departments confirmed last week that they’re working together on a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, the data center firm where Alice Huang was a top executive. Plus, the newly reinstated Nvidia CEO is still set to give congressional testimony about his role in what lawmakers call a possible national security breach.

Meanwhile, at Nvidia HQ: The espionage drama isn’t the only cloud over Huang’s unexpected return. A recent New York Times report says he regularly humiliated staff, made violent threats, and once even vowed to urinate on an employee’s brain. A former Nvidia senior VP of human resources previously described Huang’s conduct as “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behavior” he’d ever seen on the job (and warned it could get Nvidia sued).

Bottom line: Huang, for his part, said he’s taking back his old job “with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.” But he returns to a company with a more watchful board, and he’s under the public microscope now more than ever. —WK

item.title: Apple finally RSVPs to the AI agent party
item.dc:creator: Lindsey Choo
item.description: The company is building an AI agent to run your devices for you, but its track record with Siri so far has been bumpy.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: AI agents are the tech industry’s latest obsession, and Apple is now getting in on the game. While the company is fashionably late, its reputation for privacy could give it an edge. Whether it can deliver is another question, given Siri AI’s rocky rollout.

What happened: Apple is building a proactive, agentic AI assistant, per several job listings spotted by Bloomberg. Here’s what that means in human terms: “Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” one listing reads. That includes browsing the web, writing code, using apps, and calling services for you.

Apple is eyeing a launch as soon as late next year, per Bloomberg—but it’s already playing catch-up: Meta’s Muse has held the No. 2 spot on the list of free apps in Apple’s App Store since its debut (after premiering at No. 1).

Privacy, please: Apple seems to be paying attention to the mounting concerns over AI agents’ access. In its job listings, the company says agents that can “run code, use credentials, and act on a user’s behalf need strong permission models,” plus sandboxing (keeping the AI in its own fenced-off space), and transparency (whatever that means).

More Stories

AI

AI shall not pass

Tech Business

The “just kidding” heard around the world

Consumer Electronics

Turning the page on my old Kindle

It’s also holding rivals’ agents to that standard already—the latest macOS beta warns users before they let outside AI agents take over their Macs, and turning on ChatGPT’s Mac controls now takes 14 whole steps, up from four. (Apple claims it’s for security; rivals say it’s attempting to slow the competition.)

Siri-ously though: Apple’s foray into AI has so far been…underwhelming. Its upgraded Siri arrived about two years behind schedule, and it’s still working out the kinks. This month, Apple opened the assistant to developers so it can take actions inside third-party apps, like changing your ride-share pickup spot. But Siri still stumbles on the basics: In a test of the Apple HomeView smart display, Siri gaslit tech journalist Joanna Stern by insisting it didn’t have a camera (it does), among other baffling blunders.

The rest of the agent world isn’t doing much better, though—Muse reportedly read a Meta employee’s encrypted Signal messages (Signal said today it will start restricting screenshots to keep agents out). According to Reuters, Muse also messaged some employees about things they never did, and announced bank balances unprompted, some of which didn’t belong to its users (it’s unclear whether they were someone else’s or completely made up).

Bottom line: Building an agent right into its devices could give Apple a leg up, as long as it learns from Siri’s growing pains. —LC

Also in AI agents…

  • This Apple frenemy is already beating the company to the punch by letting its AI agent use your Mac for you, from filling out forms to organizing files. (Let’s see whether Apple makes the setup for it as long as a grocery list.)

item.title: Turning the page on my old Kindle
item.dc:creator: Lindsey Choo
item.description: We review two of the new Kindles.
item.content:encoded:
Disclosure: Companies may send us products to test, but they never pay for our opinions. Our recommendations are unbiased and unfiltered, and Tech Brew may earn a commission if you buy through our links.

I’m a certified e-reader loyalist: I want to carry a hefty fantasy novel without staring at my glowing phone, and I want it to fit in my tiny purse. I’ve hung on to my old Kindle Basic 2019 for years for the most boring reason possible—nothing is wrong with it.

I was skeptical that a new Kindle could improve my life, since my old one was doing the job just fine. But then I saw the lineup’s new colors and sleek redesign, and suddenly “if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it” sounded like something my husband made up.

How we tested them: Over a month, I read at least two full-length books each on the Kindle Colorsoft ($320) and Paperwhite ($250) Signature Editions, one with the Page-Turn Cover ($80) on and one without. I brought them with me everywhere—on the subway, to coffee shops, to the park, and to bed. I borrow most of my books from my local library through the Libby app, so I just sent them straight to my Kindle account, and they synced to every Kindle I own. The cover, which snaps on magnetically, has physical buttons I can press to turn pages. And to see what color actually adds, I flipped through a cookbook on the Colorsoft.

The Good: Both Kindles are very customizable—you can tweak the font, brightness, and warmth to your liking. They also respond much faster to the touch, and library books that used to take a few minutes to load on my old Kindle showed up almost immediately. The battery life was impressive: Each device still had more than half of its battery left after reading the two books, while my old Kindle tapped out every two books or so. The colors on the Colorsoft were slightly muted but plenty vivid for book covers and visual elements.

The Bad: At 7 inches, the new Kindles are a bit bigger than my old 6-inch one. That’s great for screen space, but as they’re made of aluminum, it also means they’re heavier: At 8.1 ounces, they weigh about 2 ounces more (roughly the weight of a tennis ball) than my old one, and are harder to hold with one hand. Having physical buttons with the cover is lovely, but the default button setup was so annoying (the top button turns forward, which forced me to reach my thumb up each time) that I had to dig into the settings to swap them. At $80, the cover felt more like a nice-to-have than a game changer (it’s also only compatible with the already pricier Signature Editions).

Verdict: ✅ Signal—for the Paperwhite (for everyday readers) and Colorsoft (for pretty gadget lovers). ❌ Noise—for the Page-Turn Cover, which didn’t earn its price tag. —LC

item.title: How a $1 billion video game simulates real life
item.dc:creator: Whizy Kim
item.description: The GTA series is famous for featuring crimes and violence. But the latest entry also simulates the more banal side of life, in what might be one of the biggest, most ambitious games ever.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: This isn’t your grandma’s Grand Theft Auto game (but, ironically, it might be the one she’s most interested in). The latest installment in the series, which came out today, appears to be a life simulator that pushes the limits of how obsessively detailed a virtual world can be. And it involves plenty of sharp satire on all the tech we use every day.

What happened: This is how big a moment Grand Theft Auto VI is: Already nearing an estimated $2 billion in revenue, the game (which retails for $79.99 for the standard edition) is now projected to earn more in its launch week than Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour did in 21 months. And while the series is famous as a virtual playground for stealing cars and committing other chaotic crimes, the newest entry is much more than that: It lets you live a whole other life doing chores, doomscrolling, and pursuing hobbies in its fictional version of Florida.

Here’s a taste of all the law-abiding activities in the game:

  • Doing home renovation, from fixing the leaky roof to painting your bedroom wall.
  • Going bird-watching (there are 62 different avian species to log).
  • If you’d rather not touch grass, you can scroll social media on your extremely detailed in-game smartphone (called an iFruit, naturally).
  • Oh, and you can go Jet Skiing with a dog—who, by the way, is driving the thing (which might admittedly be less law-abiding).

Uncanny valley: Every GTA game is a biting satire of society, and in 2026, that means a world littered with knockoffs of all the tech we use. Aside from the aforementioned iFruit phone, GTA VI’s version of Amazon is called Sahara; instead of Uber, there’s a rideshare app called RydeMe, and an app called BuckMe works like your mobile banking app (with Zelle). There’s even an AI-powered car scanner that flags which vehicles have GPS trackers and what their resale value would be.

How fake Florida got built: Cramming this much detail into one game is arguably a technological feat in itself. GTA VI reportedly cost more than $1 billion and took an army of nearly 5,000 people about a decade to make. Rockstar, the game’s developer, even set up a separate office just to create its roughly 30,000 unique NPCs—the non-playable characters who populate the background of the world. The game has over 600,000 animations for characters to act out, and the physics are so realistic that individual strands of hair react to movement. And, per Rockstar, no generative AI was used to create this level of fidelity.

Bottom line: Unfortunately, GTA VI is hard to play in its full glory right now. The PlayStation 5 Pro, the console that runs it best, is nearly impossible to find at retail price. But, given all the hype and its blockbuster sales, you’ll probably be hearing about it for a while, even if you never go for a drive yourself. —WK

item.title: The global chatbot friend map
item.dc:creator: Whizy Kim
item.description: A new Gallup study finds that about a third of young people now turn to AI for company—though it also depends a lot on where, exactly, you live.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: Would you ever call an AI chatbot your bestie? A new Gallup study shows how young people around the world are using AI—including how many now use it for companionship. But views on the tech vary depending on where they live, with young Americans a lot more wary of it than their peers in other countries.

What happened: Gallup’s deep dive into the lives of young people homes in on how they find social connection in an increasingly online, screen-filled world. For a surprising number, apparently, the answer is their friendly neighborhood AI chatbot.

Of nearly 16,000 people between 15 and 22 years old surveyed across 16 countries, about a third say they’ve used AI as a companion. And even if you only use Claude to vibe code personal apps, that could become a gateway to one day telling it all about your day: The more people use AI, the more they tend to become engaged “with the social side of it,” one of the study’s researchers told Wired.

Here’s how the data shakes out around the world:

  • Almost 40% of Brazilian youths use AI daily—compared to just a fifth of young people in the US, UK, and Canada.
  • Young Australians and Japanese were the most likely to use AI for friendship, while young Kenyans were the least likely.
  • Aussies were also most likely to rate AI companionship as high quality, while those in Poland were least likely to say their bot friends were BFF material.

Chicken, meet egg: Unsurprisingly, Gallup’s study found that young people who use AI for companionship were more likely to report loneliness than those who don’t. But we don’t know if those who already feel alone flock to a chatbot for a sympathetic ear or whether the tech might actually deepen social isolation in some cases. (One recent study found that AI companions can help some people feel less lonely—but only if the user perceives the AI as attentive and finds that it can “engage in a non-judgmental way.”)

What’s your location?: How people feel about AI varies greatly based on where they live. And young Americans, for one, have gotten frostier toward it lately: In a Pew survey from September, 55% of Americans ages 18 to 34 said they’re more concerned than excited about AI, up from 40% in 2024.

Bottom line: A Gallup researcher told Wired that “it wouldn’t be surprising” if AI friendships became more widespread over the next five years. Still, the most common way young people cope with loneliness, per the study, isn’t gabbing with a friend (human or bot)—it’s watching or scrolling through online content. —WK

item.title: Protests outside NYC offices of Palantir, Google denounce data centers, facial recognition tech
item.dc:creator: Tricia Crimmins
item.description: The events were part of weeklong anti-Big Tech demonstrations across the US.
item.content:encoded:
Palantir’s unmarked NYC office usually flies under the radar, but it was hard to miss on Wednesday morning when hordes of protesters gathered outside it to condemn the tech company’s work with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The demonstration was a part of a weeklong anti-Big Tech movement percolating across the US, organized by activist groups like Make the Road, United Ratepayers, Food & Water Watch, and People’s Action Institute. “Dump Big Tech” is aimed at tech giants like Palantir, OpenAI, and Google; elected officials in New York, New Jersey, California, Nevada, and Pennsylvania; and data center construction sites in Oregon and West Virginia. The protests point to souring public sentiment surrounding Big Tech, especially ahead of midterm elections.

While each protest is centered on different issues, the event outside Palantir’s offices was squarely focused on the company’s connection with ICE. Speakers at the rally said they’re scared that ICE is using Palantir’s technology to surveil immigrant communities.

“My community has felt a sense of fear that no one should have to feel,” Faith, a youth organizer for Make The Road, an immigrant justice group, told the crowd. (Organizers asked that Faith be identified only by her first name for her safety.) “Palantir working with ICE makes me worry deeply about privacy and about people getting caught up in systems that don’t feel fair, transparent, or humane.”

More Stories

AI

A week of "Dump Big Tech" protests

Tech Business

The “just kidding” heard around the world

AI

Apple finally RSVPs to the AI agent party

Because of fears about Palantir using its facial recognition technology against protesters, a majority wore disposable masks, while others wore paper masks decorated with the faces of cartoon characters and superheroes that obscured their entire visage.

“That’s a big fear, that a lot of our data and our identities [will] be tracked by Palantir because we’re here, or because we’re against the violence that ICE is enacting,” Jennifer, a Make the Road organizer who declined to share her surname, told us. “We know that it’s happening across the board, not only to undocumented people. US citizens that are speaking up are being tracked.”

She said she and other protesters hoped the demonstrations encourage elected officials to “look into the contracts” the government has with Big Tech companies and “undo all of the massive surveillance and use of AI that’s only hurting communities.”

NY Assemblymember Claire Valdez, who recently won the Democratic nomination for a US House seat in New York’s 7th Congressional District, also spoke at the rally and offered alternative uses for AI and the advanced technology coming out of companies like Palantir.

“This technology should be used to make our lives better. It should be used to shorten our working hours. It should be used to make our productivity actually pay us more. It should be used to tackle the real emergencies that we are facing right now, like climate change. Instead it is being used by billionaires and tech oligarchs to tear our communities apart,” Valdez said. “We are not going to take it anymore…While Palantir is surveilling us, we are watching them.”

At another demonstration a few blocks away in front of Google’s NYC offices earlier that day, protesters chastised the company for its data centers’ considerable water, energy, and potential fossil fuel usage. Protester Zack Winestine, part of the Rise and Resist direct action group, said he was also demonstrating against “unregulated AI” and Google specifically “forcing people to use AI” when using its search engine.

“AI is not inevitable. There’s all this hype that it can’t be stopped. That’s nonsense. People have agency. People have the right to determine how their lives will be lived and under what circumstances technology functions in their lives,” Winestine told us. “We can affect how these things develop.”

item.title: Google exec says link lists aren’t going away as search transforms
item.dc:creator: Patrick Kulp
item.description: Google VP of Search Liz Reid discussed how the search experience is changing in the AI era and what it means for the internet as a whole.
item.content:encoded:
In recent months, AI has fundamentally changed what it means to google something—and the transformation isn’t done.

The search engine made a slew of announcements at its developer conference earlier this year that included the first change to the search box in a quarter century. The upshot is a more AI-centric experience with options for news alert-style information agents that automatically scour the web for you.

Though Google has clarified that the familiar list of links isn’t going away, multiple headlines have called it the end of search as we know it. But Reid insisted that Google still cares about the health of the internet as a whole.

“Search is not a useful product if the web is not a thriving product, and so I think we probably care about that more than any other company in the world,” Google VP of Search Liz Reid told us.

We spoke with Reid about what this means for how you browse the web, what it means for websites that depend on Google for survival, and how it will change the ads you see.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Do you think that there’s a time in the future, amid all this AI change, that the familiar list of links could go away entirely? Or that there could be a different format for funneling users to the web?

I don’t see any time in which the links go away. I think what we actually see is that people don’t want AI or the web; they want both. There’s a lot of topics where AI really gets you started, and then people want to engage more. They value the expertise, the opinions, the taste of how to think about a particular topic. This is a time in which AI is growing, and it’s a time in which newsletters and podcasts and videos and all these new formats seem to also be blossoming because people really want to hear that expertise. So we want to continue to make that thrive.

We have for a long time continued to innovate on how you can surface links on the web. So we have the blue links, but we have, at times, we have the top stories part. We have what people are saying in AI Mode and in AI Overviews.

If we know users want to connect to that information, how do we make it as easy as possible? How do we make it as seamless as possible? And we’ll continue to innovate and we announced some updates pretty recently on how we’re showcasing links in additional ways. But I think that is kind of what makes search at its heart—not just knowing the information about the web, but connecting people to content on the web. And I don’t see that going away.

Obviously, online publishers are seeing click-through rates decline with these changes, and some publishers are even considering blocking all Google crawlers. In terms of making sure that the open web is still a healthy place to supply these AI tools and search, how do you think about that in the long term?

More Stories

Platforms

Google needs you to please click on its links

Tech Business

The “just kidding” heard around the world

AI

Apple finally RSVPs to the AI agent party

We do spend a lot of time thinking about this. We try to really design our AI experiences in sort of a web-forward way. We have teams whose job is to think about: What are great links to surface more effectively? How do you show them in a way that’s great for folks? We’ve innovated; one example is in AI Overviews, we’ll now often show on some timely stories, a big carousel of publishers that we didn’t have three months ago. So we’re constantly trying to figure out how we innovate on that.

The good news is that people still want to connect with other people’s content, and so we can facilitate that. And as long as people make great content that other people want to read, then we believe we can continue to foster that.

Companies like Microsoft are experimenting with publisher marketplaces or other compensation schemes. Is that something you’re considering?

We have a blog post in which we’ve talked about some of the various news deals and other things we have.

We have a variety of different ways—we have a long history of deals with news and others for great content. In general, we’re all still—I mean, at times it can feel like a long time—but we’re still pretty early in the space, and so continue to innovate.

In terms of the revenue side, how has this changed Google’s ad model? Do you feel like you’ve kind of cracked advertising in generative AI?

What we are seeing is as people ask longer queries, they’re specifying more of their intent. What are they really trying to do? What’s important to them? And that sort of allows new opportunities to think about ads targeting.

There’s some efforts like direct offers, in which…the advertiser can give a more specific ad for you based on what it is. And so, an example is like you’re searching for a hotel, you’re searching with a family. Maybe a hotel wants to offer free breakfast. They’re not going to give free breakfast to the person that they think is traveling for business who will just pay, or they won’t eat. But this family might pick that hotel because of it, and so Google’s system will allow [the hotel] to say, “Oh, I have a special discount just for you for breakfast,” and that really provides new value to the user and sort of allows the hotel to get additional visitors. We both have something that’s working, and there’s lots of room for innovation going forward.

There’s always been some level of slop on the internet, and I know Google has tools to sift through that. But as generative AI tools have created this ability to churn out more content, how do you make sure that with things like the AI Overviews, the accuracy is maintained? And have you seen the accuracy of those go up overall?

To your point, there’s always been slop. Sometimes people are like, “Oh, there’s now slop on the web.” In my experience, there’s been slop for 20 years. So we have a lot of experience and teams whose job is to ensure that both we’re getting rid of spam and that that rarely surfaces, and that high-quality content continues to surface. And when we do AI Overviews or AI Mode, we actually make use of those underlying search ranking systems so that it’s the highest-quality sites going into AI Overviews. Overall, the quality of the AI Overviews has continued to improve and has improved considerably since we first launched. The models are much better, for one, so that really helps. But also, we’ve just learned a lot and continue to grow on what the techniques are [and] how you work with the models to ensure that you can actually really ground the data in high-quality information.

Are Gemini and AI Mode search still different experiences, or are they converging into the same thing?

We think of them as having two different North Stars. Gemini is really focused on being this assistant, and search AI Mode is really focused on a generative AI search experience. And so for search, that means the importance of connecting to the web is vital. And so the way that we show the web is different…we tend to focus on information use cases more heavily. Versus with Gemini, we’ll focus on a lot of productivity and creativity use cases.

The use cases overlap. We have a view that you should meet users where you are, so you don’t go and say, like, “Oops, you asked the question in the wrong product. Try again.” We will try and answer across both of them the full breadth of questions that come to our products, but we will tune them differently, and really tune search to focus on optimizing for information use cases and optimizing for connecting people to the web.

Where is Google search headed in the long term, and what are some of the biggest ways we can expect it to change further?

There’s a couple of things that we see. Experiences are becoming more personal and custom for you, for each one. It’s not just that you can ask that longer question, but that we start to understand how to make information most useful for you. We see people learn differently. We have people who love videos and people who hate videos. We have people who are experts in the financial jargon and not in the medical jargon. We have people who speak different languages.

And so, with some of the things like generative UI…the job is not just for you to technically access information, but for it to be useful to you—that’s an important part of the mission. How do we present information in ways that are much more useful? That sense of building a thing that feels designed for you, and not just designed for 2 billion people, to make it easier for you to understand and grasp the information will continue.

Also, agents and how they show up in search in terms of just, how do they offload more of the work you don’t want to do? I think people have parts of searching where they enjoy and they’re delighted, and then they have parts of tasks that feel like there’s a lot of toil. And so, how can you offload those parts, and then make it easy for people to spend their time on the things they want to enjoy?

We’ll see that people will ask harder and harder questions. That’s been the evolution of search. You get better at answering the question. They’re like, “OK, I’m gonna raise the bar on you,” and so I think we’ll continue to see people go more and more to, what’s the real question they’re trying to get done, what’s the task they’re trying to get done.

item.title: This startup wants a robot to change your tires
item.dc:creator: Jordyn Grzelewski
item.description: One of the problems ATI aims to help solve is a growing shortage of automotive service technicians.
item.content:encoded:
Getting your car’s tires changed is the automotive service equivalent of getting a root canal.

That’s how Andy Chalofsky, CEO of newly launched AI and robotics company Automated Tire, Inc., or ATI, thinks of it—and why he and his fellow co-founders decided to use an emerging technology to disrupt a process that’s historically been cumbersome, time-consuming, and physically demanding.

“While the auto industry has made great strides with advanced technologies over recent decades, automotive service bays have seen little innovation to match,” Chalofsky said in a statement Tuesday announcing ATI’s emergence from stealth.

“Most notably, electric vehicles wear through tires up to 30% faster,” he added. “The proliferation of EVs creates significantly more tire service opportunities, but tire technician jobs are dirty, injury-prone, and difficult to fill.”

Get smart: Enter SmartBay, ATI’s platform that uses robotics, machine learning, and computer vision to automate services including tire changes, wheel balancing, and vehicle inspections. The startup touts SmartBay as a way to increase repair shops’ efficiency, improve the customer experience, and help solve a nagging automotive technician shortage.

Here’s how it works: Once a vehicle is in position, the platform automatically begins an inspection. It analyzes tire and wheel conditions while gathering diagnostic data. “The robotic system then executes the tire change and wheel balancing process, removing and reinstalling tires with consistent accuracy while simultaneously calculating and applying precise wheel weights to ensure optimal balance,” according to a news release.

More Stories

AI

The day the robotaxis froze

Tech Business

The “just kidding” heard around the world

AI

Apple finally RSVPs to the AI agent party

According to ATI, SmartBay allows one technician to manage up to three service bays at a time, reducing the time for a full tire service job by half. The product fits within a standard 12-foot service bay.

So tire-d: Chalofsky represents the fourth generation of his family to work in the tire business. He started working in tire distribution and went on to establish an online tire retailer that he later sold. In 2020, he said, he started to think about the next industry challenge he wanted to focus on.

“We just saw that there was a real need in installation, and tire changing and wheel balancing,” he told us. “It’s not a very pleasurable customer experience. We would talk to the shops and the shops would oftentimes talk about how hard it was to get labor.”

ATI cited a report from the National Automotive Dealers Association identifying a shortage of 37,000 automotive service technicians. This shortage affects drivers, ATI argued, by leading to “inconsistent service quality and even more grueling wait times.”

“We’re making not only that technician more efficient—we’re making them more profitable for them and the shop. And we’re also making it an easier job with a lower threshold of skill,” Chalofsky said. “You’re now taking the workforce and you’re allowing them to fill in the gap a little bit and do a job they’d actually rather do.”

He noted that repair shops and dealers employ highly skilled mechanics who are trained to work on vehicles that are becoming ever more complex. Rather than having these skilled workers do tire changes and vehicle inspections, they can focus on more lucrative and specialized service jobs.

“By segmenting that work, we’re allowing those…technicians to really focus on the more complicated vehicles and the more complicated problems,” Chalofsky said.

Problem, meet solution: Chalofsky believes that starting with a problem, then devising a solution, differentiates ATI’s approach from other tech startups.

“The most common tech story is these smart people that are into robotics or into engineering. They’re solving problems, and then they’re taking it to an industry to try to get a product-market fit,” he said. “The thing that defines us is the opposite: We have robotics and engineering talent, of course, but are really founded with deep automotive tire expertise. And we focused on solving a problem and bringing engineering to that problem, rather than engineering and then trying to bring the industry to the problem.”

item.title: Is it really the end of SaaS as we know it?
item.dc:creator: Patrick Kulp
item.description: New AI agent and coding tools have triggered a “SaaS-pocalypse” narrative. The reality is more complicated.
item.content:encoded:
Are software companies like Oracle and Salesforce headed for the trash icon of history?

Investors have been dumping their stocks in software-as-a-service (SaaS) companies since late January, with one trader (and dozens of headlines) dubbing it the “SaaS-pocalypse.” So while time will tell whether the end is actually nigh, change is in the air. And like seemingly all things business-related in 2026, that change is predicated on some form of AI.

The prevailing theory behind the sell-offs seems to be that sophisticated workplace agents as well as new coding tools from Anthropic and OpenAI could make this sort of business software model obsolete. If an IT team can easily “vibe code” internal software or assign tasks to role-specific plug-ins within Claude Cowork, do they still need expensive pay-per-seat platform subscriptions?

“The thing with agentic systems is now you can have agents just read your business policies and generate the software,” Booz Allen chief technology officer Bill Vass told us. “This is going to disintermediate these SaaS vendors and these ERP vendors. The market just realized that, and that’s the reason you see the big reaction.”

SaaS leaders claim a lot happens behind the scenes of these platforms that their customers can’t easily replicate, such as data governance and security and teams of developers that ensure that software works reliably. But business leaders at companies like Walmart and LiveRamp have told us they’re now building more internal tools and doing so more quickly than ever, if not yet severing SaaS contracts.

What nobody denies is that the SaaS industry is in a period of flux, and companies need to continually evolve to keep offerings competitive.

This sentiment is not exactly new. For instance, when we spoke a year ago with Scott Snyder, senior fellow at the Wharton School, he warned that SaaS companies could struggle to keep up with AI development tools.

“People could say, ‘Well, why am I using a service—[like] a Salesforce customer service bot—when I can just build my own at a very low cost because I’ve already got the AI infrastructure set up?’” Snyder said last March. “If the switching costs aren’t that high, these larger companies may roll out their own, and I think that’s going to be the interesting tension going forward.”

A major evolution

In a way, what comes next could harken back to an earlier model of business software development, according to Vass. Before standardized enterprise resource planning (ERP) software platforms became widespread in the 1990s—a precursor to SaaS—businesses mostly used custom-built internal software, Vass said.

“Originally, we all built custom ERP systems for everyone. So you did it exactly the way the Army wanted…or exactly the way Bank of America wanted, or exactly the way BMW wanted,” Vass said. “Then there was this move that, ‘Well, gee, that’s really expensive to build all those custom systems. Let’s all standardize on SAP or PeopleSoft or Oracle.’…It was very painful to go through that, and every single business person hated it.”

Apple finally RSVPs to the AI agent party

Vass said that the rise of AI agents and coding tools could swing the pendulum back toward more individual customization.

Still, Vass said he thinks many SaaS vendors will likely successfully pivot to selling AI agents, and internal agentic systems haven’t matured to the point where he’s seen companies actually cutting SaaS contracts.

“You’re going to have a combination of people that are going to just build their own agentic, if you like, ERP systems that will still be running on a cloud, probably, but run [on premises], too,” Vass said. “You’ll have others that will say, ‘I’ll just go use Agentforce from Salesforce,’ for example, or something like that, which is an agentic system to do what I do. And then it’s a lot more flexible.”

Those contracts may soon be changing form, however. Faisal Masud, who heads HP’s digital and lifecycle services division within the company’s SaaS business, said that the traditional seat- and usage-based models for pricing SaaS platforms are “evolving.” Masud said HP is mulling an additional option for outcome-based pricing based on metrics like number of tickets eliminated or hardware procurement costs.

“We’re considering, as the market evolves, to have both seat-based and outcome-based pricing models,” Masud said.

Enterprise SaaS price increases have been significantly outpacing CIO budgets in recent months, according to Gartner research, with companies often facing 10% to 20% hikes during contract renewals. Gartner expects enterprise software spending to increase by 15% this year, but much of it will go toward price increases and AI infrastructure spend, per the B2B-focused hub SaaStr.

The average annual contract value for private SaaS companies has trended upward in recent years, jumping from a median of $22,357 to $26,265 between 2023 and 2024, according to a survey of more than 1,000 respondents conducted by lending firm SaaS Capital.

Masud said the SaaS market is in for a correction rather than a full-on doomsday scenario. He said smaller point solutions for specialized use cases—“you can guess what those are”—are more likely to be impacted than larger, more integrated platforms. He predicted the biggest effect will be drops in pricing as CIOs negotiate better deals.

“Having built a SaaS company, we were users of SaaS, too…And some of those prices were just completely out of bounds for us and for the economic buyers. Everything was very expensive,” he said.

Back-SaaS

In early February, two CNBC reporters with no coding experience vibe-coded a clone of a dashboard from project-management platform Monday.com in under an hour to demonstrate the threat that SaaS companies face. The result was a working prototype that the reporters said could successfully manage their personal lives. If reporters could vibe-code their way through a dashboard, what then of the multibillion-dollar SaaS companies?

Alexey Korotich, chief product officer at workplace platform Wrike, a competitor of Monday.com, said it’s been easy to build dashboards like that for years—the user interface part of the SaaS offering is already heavily commoditized. What’s harder to replicate, he said, are data governance, back-end infrastructure, and reliability.

“Yes, you can build a whiteboard dashboard in an hour or so, but then, how does that look if you start adding features? How does that look if you start finding bugs here and there?” Korotich said. “You will quickly realize that it’s beyond your capacity to handle. It’s not one person’s job, it’s a team’s job to actually take care of this whole thing.”

Tamar Yehoshua, chief product and AI officer at Atlassian, the company behind platforms like Jira, Rovo, and Trello, said the AI transformation will likely be similar to how cloud services changed software tools, but at an accelerated pace. Cloud services first gave rise to SaaS in the aughts as subscription models replaced traditional perpetual licenses.

“SaaS is not going away,” she said. “People are going to have to build software. People are going to have to communicate with other people. Unless you think that every organization is going to be one person who’s just shooting off an AI.”

Not everyone agrees that the “SaaS-pocalypse” is an overreaction, however. Tatyana Mamut, a former Salesforce VP who now runs a startup called Wayfound that partners with Salesforce on agent monitoring, expects the SaaS market to majorly shrink over the next half-decade.

This outcome would contradict various market research reports that show the SaaS industry continuing to grow significantly in the next decade amid an ongoing AI transformation.

AI will eliminate the primary switching costs of retraining humans (since much of the work will be done by agents) and restructuring data (because LLMs don't require structured data), she said. Reductions in seats required for most SaaS subscriptions will also eat into profits, she said.

“The way we’re going to know who’s going to be alive in 2030 is to see who launches really great AI agents that are doing full and complete jobs this year in 2026,” Mamut said. “That’s my best bet.”

item.title: Big Tech money didn’t talk this election
item.dc:creator: Lindsey Choo
item.description: Voters pushed back against data centers and billionaire donors in the US midterms.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: Tech billionaires were among the biggest losers of the US midterm elections, with Elon Musk at the front of the pack. As it turns out, voters did Pokémon Go to the polls to push back on the data centers fueling the AI boom. The results could slow the AI buildout for the next several years—and send tech companies looking for friendlier ground abroad (or in orbit).

What happened: Silicon Valley’s top donors poured hundreds of millions of dollars into candidates who mostly lost. Despite spending nearly half a billion dollars backing Republicans (the most a noncandidate has ever spent), Musk saw his picks lose almost everywhere—most notably in key red states like Ohio and Texas (he spent over $200 million in the latter alone). AI was on the ballot across the country: 56% of voters called AI and data centers a “crucial or a major factor” in their vote, per an NBC exit poll.

Power struggle: Worries about higher electricity and water bills, as well as air and noise pollution, have fueled the data center backlash nationwide, per the Financial Times. Voters made it official yesterday: Texas, Georgia, and Ohio (three of the biggest AI data center hubs) elected Democratic governors who promised to pause or restrict data centers. At least 29 jurisdictions passed local bans or restrictions on data center projects, including one in Trenton, Ohio, that could stall Amazon’s plans for a campus there. But not every state followed suit: Florida narrowly elected a Republican governor who supports data centers.

Plan B(illionaire): Since the results started coming in, X has been on fire with memes about tech CEOs suddenly discovering their inner Democrat (see this very 2020 makeover)—and for good reason, as they have a lot riding on the AI buildout. Nvidia expects global spending on AI infrastructure to reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion a year by 2030.

If progress slows in the US, companies could turn abroad. But they haven’t exactly been welcome there, either. Finnish regulators ordered Google to halt work on two data centers last month, after it reportedly cleared about 250,000 trees before finishing environmental reviews. In Australia, a massive outback project scrapped its construction timeline after a regulator extended its review. Musk, for his part, joked last night that data centers in space are “looking pretty appealing” right now.

Bottom line: Deep pockets used to be the tech industry’s biggest advantage—but this week, they didn’t buy much (except, apparently, when the CEOs’ own pockets are on the line). —LC

Also in elections…

  • There was one tech sector that had arguably the best night…and made some people a whole lot of money.

item.title: AI is changing how you get—and keep—your job
item.dc:creator: Whizy Kim
item.description: Proton’s decision to “re-interview” existing staff is the sharpest example yet of how AI is changing how we’re evaluated at our jobs.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: Several companies this week have shown how quickly AI is upending everything about our jobs. It’s increasingly the bot you have to impress to land one, a tool you have to use in interviews—and the metric used to judge whether you deserve to keep your role.

What happened: Congrats, you (already) got the job. Now just “re-interview” for it. That’s the new hoop that privacy-focused email provider Proton is asking some staff to jump through—all to ensure they’re sufficiently AI-pilled. This interview do-over could lead to role changes and even affect “continued employment,” per a company email (though, in a Reddit comment, the firm claimed it’s “not doing layoffs and using AI as an excuse”).

While Proton is the only company we know of that’s making staff do a second audition for their jobs, it’s far from alone in using AI as a litmus test for grading employees. A larger shift is underway to sort the workers bosses think will thrive in the AI era from the ones they think will flounder.

More Stories

AI

Uber’s tokenmaxxing reality check

Tech Business

The “just kidding” heard around the world

AI

Apple finally RSVPs to the AI agent party

How AI grades you: Plenty of big firms now tie performance reviews to how well employees use AI or make using it a condition of keeping the role—from Big Tech names like Microsoft and Meta to less obvious AI converts like Shopify (where using the tech “is now a fundamental expectation of everyone”) and Coinbase (which fired engineers who didn’t quickly adopt AI coding tools last year).

How AI hires you: AI also plays a bigger role in whether job seekers get a foot in the door—partly by killing off the old filters. On at least one team at Anthropic, prospective hires no longer do the dreaded coding interview, because Claude does well enough on those puzzles that they don’t predict much about candidates anymore, per a manager at the AI lab. (And since a chatbot can produce a passable cover letter in seconds, some employers have even stopped asking for one.)

But in place of these old hurdles, candidates increasingly face…more AI. Google now lets software engineering candidates use Gemini during interviews, which tests how well they prompt, according to internal documents. And then there are all the job screens now conducted by uncanny AI avatars (just don’t piss them off)—and at McKinsey, would-be consultants have to impress a fake AI client as part of the hiring process.

Bottom line: These AI yardsticks assume that the tech makes workers better and more productive at their jobs—even though the evidence for that hasn’t quite arrived yet. —WK

item.title: AI shall not pass
item.dc:creator: Whizy Kim
item.description: From vibe-coded TV fixes to bots that handle calls to customer service, consumers are finding real uses for AI—and running into new roadblocks, too.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: For everyday people, the most compelling AI use case might be clawing back control over our devices and knocking out tedious errands. But several big companies are now shutting AI tools out of their products and services. It could be the start of a game of whack-a-mole: Consumers find a way to make AI work for them, and companies find a reason to nix it.

What happened: People keep finding novel uses for AI to remove some of life’s annoyances. The latest: vibe coding software to strip all ads and other bloatware from your smart TV. (Just look at this X user showing off a cleaner, less laggy TV screen.)

AI companies want you to make the most of their products (agentic or not), and users have taken them up on it—whether it’s by (allegedly) using ChatGPT to get out of a roughly $400 parking charge or deploying AI-coded software to expand what their existing music gear can do.

The burgeoning firewall: Unfortunately, it’s becoming harder to get AI to do what you want. Users recently noticed that Delta is now blocking third-party AI agents from booking flights, joining a growing list of services that have shut out AI bots (or at least appear to), including Amazon, Resy, and Amtrak. (Others, like Yelp, now make AI developers pay licensing fees for agent access.)

So far, companies have mostly pointed to security and customer experience as reasons for turning away AI agents. Amazon cited a “significantly degraded shopping and customer service experience” when it went after Perplexity’s shopping agent in a lawsuit late last year. (Perplexity argues there’s another reason the company takes issue with its agent: Fewer humans browsing Amazon also means fewer people seeing its ads.)

The security snag: And, to be fair, the AI blocks aren’t always intentional—sometimes agents just trip anti-fraud measures or get cut off for hammering a site with too many requests. Human customer service reps (you know, the few that still exist) report that they’re fielding a rising number of AI callers, which pose a problem because they can’t easily verify that a human authorized the bot, per Business Insider.

Bottom line: AI developers are going all out to convince people their AI tools are worth using—but an agent that struggles to book a flight or table may have people wondering what the tech is actually good for. —WK

item.title: The fast and the foundational: Execution drift
item.dc:creator: Morning Brew Creative Studio
item.description: You feel it, your team feels it, and your bottom line probably does too. Here’s how to close the gap.
item.content:encoded:
TOGETHER WITH

The drift dilemma: Speed up with AI, and cracks in your company’s foundation start to show. Get too cautious, and risk falling behind. The solution? A stronger foundation with Smartsheet.

Businesses have a need for speed to stay competitive, but before going pedal to the metal, a safety check is necessary.

AI provided the acceleration companies needed, but that rapid ramp-up means whatever process is already in place runs at a much faster rate. If the foundation that process is built on isn’t solid, that means cracks will form quicker, too.

That’s called execution drift, and if it gets out of hand, businesses could crash. No one wants that, so let’s buckle up, grab the wheel, and help you turn things around.

But before we hit the gas, let’s make sure we know which way we’re going.

Mapping it out

There’s no steering away from execution drift if you’re not entirely sure what it is. So let’s lay down some foundational knowledge.

Execution drift is the growing gap between strategy and execution. Think of it like drawing something from memory. No matter how clear the image might be in your head, details could get lost, things may not translate, and the finished product can look a lot different than the actual idea.

In a workplace, that gap exists between what leadership intends and what actually happens on the ground. If they don’t match up, expect unhappy leadership. This isn’t a new problem, either. In fact, PMI’s research found that stakeholders consider only 48% of projects fully successful, while 40% fall into a gray zone and 12% are outright failures. PMI frames this around the delivered value, but it points to the same underlying pattern.

When a company grows, reorganizes, replaces a tool, etc., gaps naturally form between intent and execution. The bigger the changes made, the more these gaps can appear. AI was a really big change.

While AI isn’t responsible for execution drift, it can compound broken or unstable foundations. AI introduces faster production, but if the foundations have issues, it just means more (pricey) mistakes get pumped out.

Costly confusion

With everyone on the same page of what execution drift is, we can speak a little more about where it shows up and how it gets so costly.

Day to day, execution drift shows up as manual translation work. That can look like chasing status updates across multiple tools, discovering two teams worked off different versions of the same plan because an update never fully propagated, or building exactly what a brief specified, only to find out the reasoning behind it changed two handoffs upstream and nobody updated what got passed down.

This game of corporate telephone is never fun. Worse than that, it forces teams to repeat the same monotonous work over and over, with very little payoff. Those repetitious processes can also chip away at engagement.

According to Gallup, disengagement and misalignment costs US businesses an estimated $450b–$550b a year in lost productivity. All the AI agents and tokens in the world can’t make up for that kind of loss. Even when leaders deploy AI, without one accurate, real-time view of what’s happening, they can’t move with confidence.

A smarter way

But all is not lost. There are ways to shore up your foundation to help close the gap.

It’s all about connected visibility. If that sounds familiar, you likely already saw our article with Smartsheet. Their MCP integration is designed to let AI talk and act directly with your work tools. Rather than disjointed AI tools repeating the same work in silos, Smartsheet connects them to live project data so AI can read, update, and act on it without manual handoffs.

That allows for your human teams to do the strategic kind of work you hired them for. When they’re not stuck in the weeds like that, they can zoom out for a more bird’s-eye view to help your company grow.

The good news: None of this requires a full rebuild, just a connected foundation. That’s where Smartsheet comes in.
